This page has two parts. The first is my academic research on party group switching in the European Parliament: two journal articles, each with its original Stata materials, CSV data and a Python port of the analysis. The second is a data engineering project from my data analytics training: a relational database of video games, reviews and sentiment scores. The tabs above lead to the technical detail for each dataset.

## Journal articles

::: {.pub-card}
### This too in moderation

**Evaluating the effect of delegate dissatisfaction on ambitious party group switching in the European Parliament**

Aaron R. Martin. *Party Politics* **29**(4), 726–740 (2023; first published online in 2022).

This article examines whether the most dissatisfied members are also the most likely to change party groups. The analysis finds that moderate ideological outliers have the highest odds of an ambitious switch, while the most extreme outliers are less likely to leave.

[Read the article](https://doi.org/10.1177/13540688221096531){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[Article PDF](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/13540688221096531){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
[Data, code and validation](party-politics.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
:::

::: {.pub-card}
### Party group collapse and strategic switching

**Party group collapse and strategic switching in the European Parliament**

Aaron R. Martin. *European Union Politics* **22**(3), 521–544 (2021).

This article distinguishes strategic party group switches from changes forced by group collapse. It examines how group institutionalization and the policy distance between members, national delegations and party groups relate to switching during 1979–2009.

[Read the article](https://doi.org/10.1177/1465116521999718){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[Open access PDF](https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/77080/1/1465116521999718.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
[Data, code and validation](eup.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
:::

Originally, I did all of my analysis using Stata. The downloads include those original Stata materials. Because I no longer have an institutional affiliation or a Stata licence, I used AI to convert the Stata .dta files into CSVs and port the analysis code to Python. The original Stata logs are retained as references for checking the results, and the replication checks are posted on each article's data page. Anyone can use the data for whatever they want, just please cite the appropriate articles (CC BY 4.0).

## Video games database

::: {.pub-card .pub-card-data}
### Video game sales, reviews and sentiment scores

**A relational SQLite database of 3,001 video games (2001–2016), combining sales figures, Metacritic critic and user reviews, gameplay variables and natural-language sentiment scores.**

I built this database for my data analytics bootcamp at DataScientest (Sorbonne). It started from a Kaggle video game sales dataset, which I cleaned and reshaped so that each game is one row. I then scraped Metacritic for metascores, critic reviews, user reviews and community gameplay ratings (difficulty, play time and completion), and scored the review text with three sentiment models (VADER, TextBlob and a Hugging Face transformer). The result is normalised into 13 linked tables.

Everything is in one file, so it can be opened directly with Python's built-in `sqlite3` module, [DB Browser for SQLite](https://sqlitebrowser.org/), DBeaver or any tool that reads SQLite.

[SQLite database (10 MB)](downloads/video-games/video_games.db){.btn .btn-primary .btn-sm}
[One row per game, CSV](downloads/video-games/video_game_vars_plus_sentiment_metrics.csv){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
[Kaggle dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/aaronrmartin/video-games-gameplay-reviews-sentiment-scores){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
[Schema and example query](video-games.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
